event.observation_text: The old fisherman sat on the bench by the market. His fishing rod rested beside him. He set a brown pouch of gold coins on the ground beside the bench. A few coins caught the light near its opening. The river ran past the houses below the market. He took his time checking his fishing tackle. The wooden stall and the bench cast shadows across the path. Then the fisherman stood, picked up his rod, and walked toward the river. He left the pouch behind. Nobody called after him.

witnesses.name: Henry
witnesses.identity: I'm Henry, and I've run the produce stall at the market here for the better part of twenty years. I know what I'm owed and what I owe, down to the last coin, and I keep it all in a book. I trusted the wrong people when I was young and it cost me more than once, so now I like to see the whole of a deal before I shake on it. In my experience money doesn't just turn up for no reason: somebody paid for it, and somebody usually wants it back. I'm fair to anyone who's straight with me, but I've learned the friendliest offer is the one worth reading twice.

served.content: I saw the old fisherman sit down on that bench by my stall with his fishing rod. He set a brown pouch of gold coins on the ground right there beside him—I could see a few coins catching the light near the opening. He took his time going through his fishing tackle, checking it over proper. Then he stood up, picked up his rod, and walked off toward the river. He left that pouch sitting there on the ground. Nobody called after him, and he didn't come back for it.

witnesses.name: Joan
witnesses.identity: My name is Joan, and I've lived in this village my whole life, in the same house by the river where I grew up. When I was young and my father was sick through a hard winter, the neighbors kept us fed without ever being asked, and never once called it charity. I go to the temple most mornings, and I've come to believe the gods do most of their work through people: a kind word, a hand held out at the right moment. I try to think the best of someone until they give me a real reason not to. Good things have a way of finding the people who are willing to see them.
